groups.text: Over three sittings you build one program: a payment ledger in memory.
Many threads move money at once, and not one cent may be lost or created.
Here it is, finished.
Each request gets a virtual thread that screens the transfer.
Then a bounded pool writes it to a journal and applies it to the accounts.
You build it from the inside out.
Each part comes from an earlier lesson, named under the diagram.
Sitting one, in Java, builds the core.
Each account has its own lock, and a transfer always locks the smaller id first, so opposite transfers can't deadlock.
The balance check sits inside both locks, with the debit and the credit.
A transfer is an immutable record, so any thread sees it whole.
And a stress test of eight threads tries hard to break it.
Sitting two, still in Java, runs the ledger on a pool you can defend: eight threads and eighty queue slots, from Little's law.
When it is full, the caller gets a five hundred three.
Each task writes the journal before it applies.
On shutdown the pool drains, and hands back every transfer that never started.
A snapshot takes every lock in id order, and publishes an immutable copy through a volatile field.
Sitting three adds the front, in Kotlin, over the same Java ledger.
Every request gets a new virtual thread, because requests mostly wait.
The slow fraud service sits behind one shared semaphore of twenty permits.
Each request has one deadline of three hundred milliseconds.
When it runs out, the fraud call is interrupted, so its permit comes back.
Fraud and limits run side by side.
The first no wins, and no check outlives its request.
Through every sitting, one rule holds.
Money moves only inside apply, under both account locks, so the sum of all balances never changes.
